<!-- slide 63 -->
# PyWaffle {.divider}

[Composition as small squares]{.eyebrow}


<!-- slide 64 -->
## Install & Import {.smaller}

[PyWaffle · setup]{.eyebrow}

### Part-of-whole, when the audience needs to *count*

A pie chart asks the eye to compare **angles**; a stacked bar asks it to compare **lengths against a shared baseline**. A **waffle** does neither — it draws **discrete tiles** and lets the eye **count units**. With a 10×10 grid, each square is exactly **1%** of the whole. Think election seats, MPs, samples in a cohort — anywhere the audience naturally counts in heads.

```bash
pip install pywaffle
```

```{.python code-line-numbers="1"}
# the only object you need from the package — pass it as FigureClass to plt.figure(...)
from pywaffle import Waffle
```

Where to reach for it: small **integer-like compositions** (5 ancestry components, 8 cell types, 6 mutation classes). Where to avoid it: continuous-like multi-sample composition with many tiny slices — use a stacked bar there instead.


<!-- slide 65 -->
## The Data {.smaller}

[PyWaffle · data peek]{.eyebrow}

### One row per population, mean K1..K5 ancestry proportion

`load_admixture()` returns 120 individuals × 5 K-components. We collapse to **one row per population** by averaging, then turn each row into a waffle.

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="46%"}
```{.python code-line-numbers="1-2|4-6|8-9"}
admix = load_admixture()                            # individual, population, K1..K5
K_cols = ["K1", "K2", "K3", "K4", "K5"]             # the five ancestry components

# collapse to population means: each row sums to ~1.0
pop_mean = admix.groupby("population")[K_cols].mean()
pop_mean = pop_mean.loc[["EUR", "AFR", "EAS", "SAS", "AMR"]]   # stable plot order

# convert proportions -> integer percentages (each row sums to ~100)
pop_pct = (pop_mean * 100).round().astype(int)
pop_pct
```
:::
::: {.column width="54%"}
```{python}
#| echo: false
admix = load_admixture()
K_cols = ["K1", "K2", "K3", "K4", "K5"]
pop_mean = admix.groupby("population")[K_cols].mean()
pop_mean = pop_mean.loc[["EUR", "AFR", "EAS", "SAS", "AMR"]]
pop_pct = (pop_mean * 100).round().astype(int)
pop_pct
```

**Read it:** EUR row ≈ {K1=high, K2..K5=low}. Each row is one waffle.
:::
::::


<!-- slide 66 -->
## Step 1 · One Waffle for EUR {.smaller}

[PyWaffle · build]{.eyebrow}

### 100 squares in a 5×20 grid — each square = 1% of EUR ancestry

`plt.figure(FigureClass=Waffle, ...)` is the special incantation: matplotlib creates the figure, but `pywaffle` takes over the drawing. We feed it the EUR percentages as a dict, five Economist colours, and a legend below the grid.

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="46%"}
```{.python code-line-numbers="1-3|5-15"}
# pull one population row and convert to a {component: percent} dict
eur = pop_pct.loc["EUR"].to_dict()                       # {"K1": ..., "K2": ..., ...}
colors = [GREEN, BLUE, AMBER, RED, PURPLE]               # one Economist colour per K

fig = plt.figure(                                         # CREATE — Waffle takes over
    FigureClass=Waffle,                                   # matplotlib hands drawing to pywaffle
    rows=5, columns=20,                                   # 5 × 20 = 100 squares, 1% each
    values=eur,                                           # CALL: counts dict
    colors=colors,                                        # one colour per K-component
    legend={"loc": "lower center",                        # legend below the grid
            "bbox_to_anchor": (0.5, -0.15),
            "ncol": 5, "framealpha": 0},
    title={"label": "EUR — ancestry composition",
           "loc": "left"},
    figsize=(7, 3))
```

The trick to read: the legend sits **below** the waffle (the chart itself is the visual), so the colours map straight onto the labels without crowding the squares.
:::
::: {.column width="54%"}
```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 3
from pywaffle import Waffle

admix = load_admixture()
K_cols = ["K1", "K2", "K3", "K4", "K5"]
pop_mean = admix.groupby("population")[K_cols].mean()
pop_mean = pop_mean.loc[["EUR", "AFR", "EAS", "SAS", "AMR"]]
pop_pct = (pop_mean * 100).round().astype(int)

eur = pop_pct.loc["EUR"].to_dict()
colors = [GREEN, BLUE, AMBER, RED, PURPLE]

fig = plt.figure(
    FigureClass=Waffle,
    rows=5, columns=20,
    values=eur,
    colors=colors,
    legend={"loc": "lower center", "bbox_to_anchor": (0.5, -0.15),
            "ncol": 5, "framealpha": 0},
    title={"label": "EUR — ancestry composition", "loc": "left"},
    figsize=(7, 3))
plt.show()
```
:::
::::


<!-- slide 67 -->
## Step 2 · Small Multiples — One Waffle Per Population {.smaller}

[PyWaffle · build]{.eyebrow}

### The `plots` kwarg packs many waffles into one figure

Instead of one big waffle, we pass `plots={…}` — a dict where each key is a subplot location (3-digit code or tuple) and each value is the kwargs for that sub-waffle. All share the same colours, so the eye can read **across rows**: K1 dominates EUR, K2 dominates AFR, and so on.

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="46%"}
```{.python code-line-numbers="1-3|5-19"}
colors = [GREEN, BLUE, AMBER, RED, PURPLE]               # shared palette across panels
pops = ["EUR", "AFR", "EAS", "SAS", "AMR"]               # one panel per population

# build the per-subplot kwargs dict; key = "151", "152", ... = 1 row × 5 cols, slot i
panels = {                                                # one entry per population
    150 + i + 1: {                                         # 1 row, 5 cols, slot i+1
        "values": pop_pct.loc[p].to_dict(),               # this pop's K dict
        "title": {"label": p, "loc": "left"},             # subplot title
    }
    for i, p in enumerate(pops)
}

fig = plt.figure(                                         # CREATE — Waffle handles layout
    FigureClass=Waffle,                                   # CALL via FigureClass
    plots=panels,                                         # all 5 sub-waffles
    rows=5, columns=10,                                   # default for every sub-panel
    colors=colors,                                        # shared colour map
    figsize=(11, 3))
```

By driving the panel dict with a comprehension we keep the build vectorised and **no manual `for-add_subplot` loop**.
:::
::: {.column width="54%"}
```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 11
#| fig-height: 3
from pywaffle import Waffle

admix = load_admixture()
K_cols = ["K1", "K2", "K3", "K4", "K5"]
pop_mean = admix.groupby("population")[K_cols].mean()
pop_mean = pop_mean.loc[["EUR", "AFR", "EAS", "SAS", "AMR"]]
pop_pct = (pop_mean * 100).round().astype(int)

colors = [GREEN, BLUE, AMBER, RED, PURPLE]
pops = ["EUR", "AFR", "EAS", "SAS", "AMR"]
panels = {
    150 + i + 1: {
        "values": pop_pct.loc[p].to_dict(),
        "title": {"label": p, "loc": "left"},
    }
    for i, p in enumerate(pops)
}

fig = plt.figure(
    FigureClass=Waffle,
    plots=panels,
    rows=5, columns=10,
    colors=colors,
    figsize=(11, 3))
plt.show()
```
:::
::::


<!-- slide 68 -->
## Step 3 · Replace Squares With Icons {.smaller}

[PyWaffle · variant]{.eyebrow}

### FontAwesome icons turn the grid into a pictogram

Swap `icons="user"` and `font_size` for the square — now each tile is a person glyph. Reach for this when the unit *is* a person, a sample, a tree. PyWaffle ships the FontAwesome free font, so no extra download is needed once `pip install pywaffle` is done.

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="46%"}
```{.python code-line-numbers="1-3|5-16"}
eur = pop_pct.loc["EUR"].to_dict()                        # one population row
colors = [GREEN, BLUE, AMBER, RED, PURPLE]                # shared palette

fig = plt.figure(                                          # CREATE
    FigureClass=Waffle,                                    # CALL via FigureClass
    rows=5, columns=20,                                    # 100 icons total
    values=eur,
    colors=colors,
    icons="user",                                          # FontAwesome glyph name
    icon_legend=True,                                      # show the icon in the legend
    font_size=14,                                          # icon size in points
    legend={"loc": "lower center",
            "bbox_to_anchor": (0.5, -0.15),
            "ncol": 5, "framealpha": 0},
    title={"label": "EUR — ancestry, one icon = 1%",
           "loc": "left"},
    figsize=(7.5, 3))
```

Other ready-to-use glyphs that fit biology: `"tree"`, `"leaf"`, `"seedling"`, `"dna"`, `"flask"`, `"microscope"`. Browse the FontAwesome free set for more.
:::
::: {.column width="54%"}
```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 7.5
#| fig-height: 3
from pywaffle import Waffle

admix = load_admixture()
K_cols = ["K1", "K2", "K3", "K4", "K5"]
pop_mean = admix.groupby("population")[K_cols].mean()
pop_mean = pop_mean.loc[["EUR", "AFR", "EAS", "SAS", "AMR"]]
pop_pct = (pop_mean * 100).round().astype(int)

eur = pop_pct.loc["EUR"].to_dict()
colors = [GREEN, BLUE, AMBER, RED, PURPLE]

fig = plt.figure(
    FigureClass=Waffle,
    rows=5, columns=20,
    values=eur,
    colors=colors,
    icons="user",
    icon_legend=True,
    font_size=14,
    legend={"loc": "lower center", "bbox_to_anchor": (0.5, -0.15),
            "ncol": 5, "framealpha": 0},
    title={"label": "EUR — ancestry, one icon = 1%", "loc": "left"},
    figsize=(7.5, 3))
plt.show()
```
:::

<!-- slide 69 -->
## Variant · Snake-Block Arrangement {.smaller}

[PyWaffle · variant]{.eyebrow}

### The same data, different fill order

By default, pywaffle fills the grid **column by column from left**. Setting `block_arranging_style="snake"` makes each colour fill a contiguous *snake* before the next one starts. The picture's *meaning* doesn't change (same totals), but the **clustering of like-colours** reads differently — bigger continuous blocks of each colour, easier to see where one category dominates.

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="46%"}
```{.python code-line-numbers="1-3|5-15"}
afr = pop_pct.loc["AFR"].to_dict()                         # pick a population with a clear K dominance
colors = [GREEN, BLUE, AMBER, RED, PURPLE]                 # same palette as before

fig = plt.figure(                                           # CREATE
    FigureClass=Waffle,                                     # CALL via FigureClass
    rows=5, columns=20,
    values=afr,
    colors=colors,
    block_arranging_style="snake",                          # new: contiguous-block fill
    legend={"loc": "lower center",
            "bbox_to_anchor": (0.5, -0.15),
            "ncol": 5, "framealpha": 0},
    title={"label": "AFR — snake fill (one big block per K)",
           "loc": "left"},
    figsize=(7, 3))
```

If `block_arranging_style="snake"` is not recognised on older pywaffle versions, try the default mode (no kwarg) and compare side-by-side. The intent is the same: make the dominant category one big contiguous slab.
:::
::: {.column width="54%"}
```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 3
from pywaffle import Waffle

admix = load_admixture()
K_cols = ["K1", "K2", "K3", "K4", "K5"]
pop_mean = admix.groupby("population")[K_cols].mean()
pop_mean = pop_mean.loc[["EUR", "AFR", "EAS", "SAS", "AMR"]]
pop_pct = (pop_mean * 100).round().astype(int)

afr = pop_pct.loc["AFR"].to_dict()
colors = [GREEN, BLUE, AMBER, RED, PURPLE]

try:
    fig = plt.figure(
        FigureClass=Waffle, rows=5, columns=20,
        values=afr, colors=colors,
        block_arranging_style="snake",
        legend={"loc": "lower center", "bbox_to_anchor": (0.5, -0.15),
                "ncol": 5, "framealpha": 0},
        title={"label": "AFR — snake fill (one big block per K)", "loc": "left"},
        figsize=(7, 3))
except TypeError:
    # older pywaffle: fall back to default arrangement
    fig = plt.figure(
        FigureClass=Waffle, rows=5, columns=20,
        values=afr, colors=colors,
        legend={"loc": "lower center", "bbox_to_anchor": (0.5, -0.15),
                "ncol": 5, "framealpha": 0},
        title={"label": "AFR — default fill", "loc": "left"},
        figsize=(7, 3))
plt.show()
```
:::
::::


<!-- slide 70 -->
## PyWaffle · Takeaway {.smaller}

[PyWaffle · recap]{.eyebrow}

### Squares the audience can count.

::: {.takeaway}
[The recipe]{.tl}
1. **Prep one row of counts** per panel — a `{category: integer}` dict that sums near 100.
2. **`plt.figure(FigureClass=Waffle, rows=..., columns=..., values=..., colors=...)`** — that's the chart.
3. **Small multiples via `plots={...}`** — one sub-waffle per group, shared colours.
4. **`icons="user"`** to turn squares into FontAwesome pictograms when the unit is a person/sample/tree.

**When to reach for it.** Part-of-whole, categories are **non-ordinal**, and the audience naturally **counts in units** (seats, MPs, samples). Compare with the **stacked bar** from day-2 `_01`: a stacked bar is the right tool when you need to compare composition **across many individuals** along a shared axis; a waffle is for telling **one composition's story** with weight.
:::
